summary: This unit covers inflammation of the kidney interstitium and bladder that is not a primary glomerular disease: drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy with papillary necrosis, chronic and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, and interstitial cystitis. Exam items give a drug history or a scarred kidney and ask you to name the lesion, its cause, and what it will do to renal function.

points: A hypersensitivity reaction (mostly T cell mediated, type IV) in the renal interstitium, starting days to weeks after a new drug, often about 2 weeks.
Common drugs: penicillins (classically methicillin), cephalosporins, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, diuretics (thiazides, furosemide), sulfonamides, rifampin, allopurinol.
Findings: fever, rash, eosinophilia, rising creatinine, pyuria with WBC casts, and sometimes eosinophils in the urine (an insensitive test).
The full triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia appears in only a minority of patients.
Histology: interstitial edema with lymphocytes, macrophages, and eosinophils; tubulitis; some drugs give small non-necrotizing granulomas; glomeruli are spared.
NSAIDs can cause AIN together with nephrotic-range proteinuria (minimal change pattern) and often without fever or rash.
Usually recovers over weeks once the drug is stopped; delay allows interstitial fibrosis.
Years of heavy use of combination analgesics (classically phenacetin with aspirin and caffeine) cause chronic interstitial nephritis with papillary necrosis.
The papillary tip is the most poorly perfused part of the kidney; aspirin blocks vasodilating prostaglandins and drug metabolites cause oxidative injury, so the papillae die first.
Cortex over a necrotic papilla then atrophies and scars, giving a chronic tubulointerstitial pattern.
Clinical: polyuria with poor concentrating ability, sterile pyuria, hematuria, slowly rising creatinine.
A sloughed papilla can pass down the ureter, causing colic and gross hematuria, or obstruct it.
Long-term phenacetin use raises the risk of urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.
Other causes of papillary necrosis: diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease or trait, severe acute pyelonephritis, and urinary obstruction.
Two main routes: reflux nephropathy from vesicoureteral reflux beginning in childhood, and chronic obstruction (stones, prostatic enlargement, strictures) with repeated infection.
Gross: coarse, irregular, often asymmetric corticomedullary scars sitting over blunted, dilated, deformed calyces.
Reflux scars favor the upper and lower poles, where compound papillae allow urine to reflux into the kidney.
Histology: interstitial fibrosis, chronic inflammation (lymphocytes, plasma cells), and atrophic dilated tubules filled with pink hyaline casts that look like thyroid follicles (thyroidization).
Clinical: hypertension, polyuria and nocturia from lost concentrating ability, slowly progressive chronic kidney disease; WBC casts during flares.
Scarred kidneys can develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with proteinuria.
A rare chronic destructive form of pyelonephritis, usually one kidney.
Typical setting: an obstructing stone (often staghorn) with Proteus or E. coli infection.
The kidney fills with yellow nodules of lipid-laden foamy macrophages, plus plasma cells, neutrophils, and giant cells.
Presents as an enlarged nonfunctioning kidney with a mass on imaging, so it can mimic renal cell carcinoma; the foamy cells can resemble clear tumor cells.
Chronic bladder or pelvic pain with urgency and frequency, with repeatedly negative urine cultures.
Most often in women; pain typically worsens as the bladder fills and eases after voiding.
A diagnosis of exclusion: rule out infection, stones, and bladder cancer first.
Cystoscopy shows Hunner lesions (red ulcerated patches) in some patients.

tricks.label: SAAD papa with papillary necrosis
tricks.text: Sickle cell disease or trait, Acute pyelonephritis, Analgesics, Diabetes mellitus.

tricks.label: New drug, then kidney rash
tricks.text: If creatinine rises 1 to 3 weeks after starting an antibiotic, PPI, NSAID, or diuretic, and the urine has WBCs and WBC casts without bacteria, think AIN before infection.

tricks.label: Coarse and lopsided versus fine and even
tricks.text: Chronic pyelonephritis gives coarse, asymmetric scars over deformed calyces. Benign nephrosclerosis gives two evenly shrunken kidneys with a fine granular surface.

highYield: Fever, rash, eosinophilia, and WBC casts about 2 weeks after starting a penicillin: drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis.
WBC casts prove the inflammation is in the kidney, as in AIN or pyelonephritis, and not only in the bladder.
Long-term combination analgesic use: papillary necrosis and higher risk of urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis.
Thyroidization of tubules with coarse scars over blunted calyces: chronic pyelonephritis.
Reflux nephropathy scars cluster at the upper and lower poles.
Staghorn stone with Proteus and a kidney full of foamy macrophages: xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, a renal cell carcinoma mimic.
Bladder pain with urgency and frequency and repeatedly negative cultures in a woman: interstitial cystitis.
pitfalls: AIN and acute pyelonephritis both give WBC casts; AIN has a drug history, eosinophils, and a sterile culture, while pyelonephritis has bacteria and flank pain.
AIN spares the glomeruli, so red cell casts point instead to glomerulonephritis.
Thyroidization is not unique to chronic pyelonephritis but, with coarse scars over deformed calyces, it is the classic picture.
A mass in a kidney with a staghorn stone may be xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, not renal cell carcinoma; the foamy cells are macrophages, not tumor cells.

Onset days to weeks after the drug, often about 2 weeks
Mostly T cell mediated hypersensitivity in the interstitium

summary: This unit covers inherited and developmental kidney disease: Alport syndrome, the cystic kidney diseases, renal agenesis, and vesicoureteral reflux. Exam items link a gene or developmental error to the kidney lesion and to findings outside the kidney, such as deafness, liver cysts, brain aneurysms, or Potter sequence.

points: Defect in type IV collagen (alpha 3, 4, or 5 chains) of the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea, and lens.
Most cases are X-linked (COL4A5), so males have more severe disease; autosomal forms also exist.
Hematuria in childhood, then proteinuria and progression to end-stage renal disease in young adulthood.
Extrarenal: sensorineural hearing loss and eye lesions, especially anterior lenticonus.
Electron microscopy: GBM thinned in places and thickened and split in others, giving a basket-weave look.
Mutations in PKD1 (polycystin-1, chromosome 16, most cases) or PKD2 (polycystin-2, chromosome 4).
Cysts grow from all parts of the nephron and slowly replace the kidney; symptoms usually start in adulthood.
Bilaterally enlarged lumpy kidneys, flank pain, hematuria, stones, infected cysts, hypertension, progressive renal failure.
Hypertension comes from cysts compressing vessels, causing local ischemia and renin release.
Extrarenal: liver cysts (most common), berry aneurysms with risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula.
Autosomal recessive PKD (PKHD1, fibrocystin): presents in infancy with bilaterally enlarged kidneys made of elongated cysts (dilated collecting ducts) at right angles to the surface.
Severe ARPKD makes little fetal urine, so oligohydramnios and Potter sequence can occur; survivors develop congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension.
Multicystic dysplastic kidney: abnormal metanephric development, often with ureteral atresia; usually one side, sporadic, and not inherited.
Dysplastic kidney contains cysts plus immature tubules, undifferentiated mesenchyme, and sometimes cartilage; the other kidney compensates.
Acquired cystic disease: many cysts in kidneys of patients on long-term dialysis, with a higher risk of renal cell carcinoma.
Failure of the ureteric bud to form or to induce the metanephric mesenchyme.
From about the second trimester, amniotic fluid is mostly fetal urine, so bilateral agenesis causes oligohydramnios.
Too little fluid compresses the fetus and stops normal lung growth: Potter sequence.
Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia (the cause of death), flat face with low-set ears and small chin, limb deformities such as clubfeet.
Unilateral agenesis is usually silent; the single kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy.
Unilateral agenesis can come with genital tract anomalies on the same side, because the ureteric bud grows out of the mesonephric duct, next to the paramesonephric duct.
Primary VUR: the ureter runs too short a course through the bladder wall, so bladder contraction does not squeeze it shut.
Secondary VUR: high bladder pressure, as with posterior urethral valves or neurogenic bladder.
Urine flows back up to the kidney during voiding, carrying bacteria: recurrent febrile UTIs and pyelonephritis in children.
Repeated infection plus intrarenal reflux causes reflux nephropathy: polar scars, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease.
Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is the diagnostic study and grades the reflux.
Often familial; mild primary reflux often resolves as the child grows and the intravesical ureter lengthens.

tricks.label: Alport: can't see, can't pee, can't hear high C
tricks.text: Eye lesions (anterior lenticonus), renal disease with hematuria, and sensorineural hearing loss, all from abnormal type IV collagen.

tricks.label: POTTER
tricks.text: Pulmonary hypoplasia, Oligohydramnios (the trigger), Twisted face, Twisted skin, Extremity defects, Renal failure in utero.

tricks.label: ADPKD in adults, ARPKD in babies
tricks.text: ADPKD shows up in adults. ARPKD shows up in newborns and brings the liver along as congenital hepatic fibrosis.

highYield: Young man with hematuria, hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus: Alport syndrome; split, basket-weave GBM on electron microscopy.
Adult with bilateral flank masses, hypertension, and a family history: ADPKD; sudden worst headache means a ruptured berry aneurysm.
Liver cysts are the most common extrarenal finding in ADPKD.
Newborn with huge kidneys, Potter facies, and later portal hypertension: ARPKD with congenital hepatic fibrosis.
Infant with one cystic nonfunctioning kidney and a normal other kidney: multicystic dysplastic kidney.
Bilateral renal agenesis: oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, death shortly after birth.
Child with recurrent febrile UTIs: test for vesicoureteral reflux with a voiding cystourethrogram.
Long-term dialysis patient with new cysts and a solid mass: renal cell carcinoma in acquired cystic disease.
pitfalls: ADPKD and ARPKD both give big cystic kidneys; age, liver fibrosis versus liver cysts, and inheritance separate them.
Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a developmental error, not an inherited disease, and is usually one-sided.
Acquired cystic disease kidneys are usually not enlarged the way ADPKD kidneys are.
Alport syndrome and reactive arthritis both have 'can't see, can't pee' mnemonics; Alport adds deafness, reactive arthritis adds joints.

ARPKD: PKHD1, infants, both kidneys
ARPKD extras: oligohydramnios, Potter sequence, congenital hepatic fibrosis
Multicystic dysplastic: not inherited, usually one kidney
Dysplasia shows immature tubules and sometimes cartilage
Acquired cystic disease: long-term dialysis
Acquired cystic disease raises renal cell carcinoma risk

No kidneys means no fetal urine
Fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid later in pregnancy

summary: This unit covers diseases of the renal blood vessels: hemolytic uremic syndrome, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, renal artery stenosis, renal infarction, sickle cell nephropathy, and renal vein thrombosis. Exam items describe a vessel lesion or a blood smear and ask you to predict what happens to the kidney, the blood pressure, or the urine.

points: Typical HUS follows bloody diarrhea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7, mostly in young children, about a week after the diarrhea starts.
Shiga toxin binds Gb3 receptors on glomerular endothelium and stops protein synthesis, injuring the endothelial cells.
Injured endothelium triggers platelet-fibrin microthrombi in glomerular capillaries and arterioles (thrombotic microangiopathy).
Triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia from platelet consumption, and acute kidney injury.
Hemolysis labs: high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, negative direct Coombs test; PT and aPTT are normal, unlike DIC.
TTP: deficient ADAMTS13 (usually an autoantibody) leaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers that clump platelets; mostly adults, more neurologic signs, milder renal injury.
Benign nephrosclerosis: long-standing hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis, a pink glassy thickening from plasma proteins leaking into the arteriolar wall.
Narrowed arterioles cause patchy ischemic loss of nephrons, so both kidneys shrink evenly with a finely granular surface.
Benign nephrosclerosis usually causes mild proteinuria and slowly progressive CKD; diabetes and aging also cause hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
Malignant hypertension (very high pressure, often above 180/120 mm Hg, with organ damage) causes hyperplastic onion-skin arteriolosclerosis.
Malignant hypertension also causes fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles and pinpoint cortical hemorrhages, the flea-bitten kidney.
Malignant hypertension presents with acute kidney injury, hematuria, proteinuria, headache, and papilledema; ischemia drives more renin, which raises pressure further.
Atherosclerotic stenosis is most common: older adults with vascular risk factors, lesion at the ostium or proximal artery.
Fibromuscular dysplasia: young women, a noninflammatory thickening of the arterial wall in the mid to distal artery, string of beads on angiography.
Low perfusion pressure at the juxtaglomerular cells raises renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone, so hypertension follows (sometimes with hypokalemia).
Clues: an abdominal or flank bruit, resistant hypertension, a rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor.
The poorly perfused kidney shrinks from ischemic atrophy, while the other kidney faces high pressure and develops nephrosclerosis.
Branches of the renal artery are end arteries without useful collaterals, so a blocked branch causes infarction.
Most come from emboli: left atrial thrombus in atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus after myocardial infarction, endocarditis vegetations; less often local thrombosis.
Pale, wedge-shaped coagulative infarct with its base at the capsule and its tip toward the hilum; it heals as a V-shaped depressed scar.
Clinical: sudden flank pain, hematuria, and a raised serum LDH.
The renal medulla is low in oxygen, very hypertonic, and acidic; all three push hemoglobin S to polymerize.
Hypertonicity pulls water out of red cells and raises the HbS concentration; acidity lowers oxygen affinity (Bohr effect), releasing more oxygen.
Sickled cells block the vasa recta, causing medullary microinfarcts and papillary necrosis.
Loss of the medullary concentration gradient leaves urine fixed near plasma osmolality (isosthenuria), causing polyuria, nocturia, and dehydration risk.
Hematuria is common, in sickle cell disease and in sickle cell trait.
Sickle cell trait is also linked to renal medullary carcinoma, a rare aggressive tumor of young people.
Causes: nephrotic syndrome (especially membranous nephropathy), renal cell carcinoma growing into the renal vein, and dehydration in infants.
Nephrotic syndrome is hypercoagulable because antithrombin is lost in the urine and the liver makes more clotting factors.
Findings: flank pain, hematuria, an enlarged swollen kidney, worsening proteinuria or renal function.
Left renal vein thrombosis can cause a left varicocele because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.

charts.title: HUS versus TTP
rows: Low ADAMTS13 leaves ultra-large vWF multimers

tricks.label: Medulla makes cells sickle
tricks.text: Low oxygen, high salt, and acid are all found in the renal medulla, and each one favors sickling. That is why even sickle trait can cause hematuria and isosthenuria.

tricks.label: Hyaline is slow, onion skin is fast
tricks.text: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis goes with years of mild hypertension and slow kidney decline. Onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis goes with malignant hypertension and acute renal failure.

tricks.label: Who gets which stenosis
tricks.text: Older smoker with a bruit points to atherosclerosis at the ostium. Young woman with hard-to-control blood pressure points to fibromuscular dysplasia with a string of beads.

highYield: Child with bloody diarrhea, then pallor, petechiae, and oliguria: HUS from E. coli O157:H7 Shiga toxin.
Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia and normal PT and aPTT: thrombotic microangiopathy (HUS or TTP), not DIC.
Low ADAMTS13 activity: TTP.
Evenly shrunken kidneys with a fine granular surface and hyaline arterioles: benign nephrosclerosis.
Flea-bitten kidney with onion-skin arterioles and fibrinoid necrosis: malignant hypertension.
Young woman with resistant hypertension and an abdominal bruit: fibromuscular dysplasia.
Atrial fibrillation with sudden flank pain and hematuria: renal infarction from an embolus.
Sickle cell trait in a young adult with painless hematuria or inability to concentrate urine: medullary sickling.
pitfalls: HUS and TTP share schistocytes and low platelets; the toxin story and kidney focus point to HUS, low ADAMTS13 and brain signs point to TTP.
DIC also has schistocytes, but PT and aPTT are prolonged and fibrinogen falls.
In renal artery stenosis, the stenotic kidney becomes small and atrophic; the other kidney shows the hypertensive damage.
Renal infarcts are pale because the kidney is a solid organ with end arteries; red infarcts are seen in organs with dual blood supply or venous occlusion.
Isosthenuria means urine fixed near plasma osmolality; it is a loss of concentrating ability, not a loss of filtration.

dumps.p: Draw a flow chart from eating undercooked ground beef to the lab results of hemolytic uremic syndrome. Add a side column showing how TTP differs.
l: E. coli O157:H7 causes bloody diarrhea
Shiga toxin enters the blood and binds Gb3 on glomerular endothelium
Toxin stops protein synthesis and injures endothelial cells
Platelet-fibrin microthrombi form in small renal vessels
Red cells are sheared into schistocytes: high LDH, low haptoglobin
Platelets are consumed: thrombocytopenia
Glomerular thrombi cause acute kidney injury
TTP: low ADAMTS13, ultra-large vWF, more neurologic signs, mostly adults

dumps.p: Draw two small kidneys side by side, one with benign nephrosclerosis and one with malignant hypertension. Under each, draw an arteriole cross section and label it.
l: Benign: both kidneys evenly shrunken, finely granular surface
Benign arteriole: hyaline arteriolosclerosis, pink glassy wall
Benign course: mild proteinuria, slow CKD
Malignant: flea-bitten surface from pinpoint hemorrhages
Malignant arteriole: concentric onion-skin layers (hyperplastic)
Malignant arteriole: fibrinoid necrosis
Malignant course: acute kidney injury, hematuria, papilledema
Ischemia raises renin and makes pressure climb further

summary: This unit covers tumors of the kidney and urinary tract: renal cell carcinoma and its subtypes, oncocytoma, Wilms tumor in children, and the carcinomas of the bladder and collecting system. Exam items lean on the classic links: the gene or syndrome behind the tumor, its look under the microscope, its paraneoplastic hormones, and its risk factors.

points: Most common renal cell carcinoma; arises from proximal tubule cells; peaks in the 60s and 70s, more often in men.
Loss of the VHL gene on chromosome 3p (sporadic and in von Hippel-Lindau disease) stabilizes HIF, which drives VEGF and other growth signals.
Gross: golden-yellow cut surface from lipid, with hemorrhage, necrosis, and cystic areas.
Micro: cells with clear cytoplasm filled with lipid and glycogen, in nests separated by a rich network of thin-walled vessels.
Risk factors: smoking (the strongest), obesity, hypertension, acquired cystic disease of long-term dialysis, von Hippel-Lindau disease.
Tends to grow into the renal vein and up the inferior vena cava, sometimes to the right heart.
Hematuria is the most common sign; the full triad of hematuria, flank pain, and flank mass is uncommon.
Often found by chance on imaging done for something else.
Paraneoplastic hormones: erythropoietin (polycythemia), PTHrP (hypercalcemia), renin (hypertension), sometimes ACTH (Cushing syndrome).
Spreads through the blood to lung (round cannonball nodules) and bone (lytic lesions), often before local symptoms appear.
A new left varicocele that does not empty when the man lies down suggests tumor blocking the left renal vein, where the left gonadal vein drains.
Papillary carcinoma: second most common, often multifocal; trisomy 7 and 17; papillae with fibrovascular cores holding foamy macrophages.
Chromophobe carcinoma: from intercalated cells of the collecting duct; pale cells with distinct cell borders and a halo around the nucleus; better prognosis.
Oncocytoma: benign tumor from intercalated cells; large pink cells packed with mitochondria; brown tumor with a central stellate scar.
Most common primary kidney cancer of children, usually ages 2 to 5 years.
Large, smooth, unilateral flank mass, sometimes with hematuria, abdominal pain, or hypertension.
Triphasic histology: blastema (small round blue cells), stroma, and epithelium forming primitive tubules and glomeruli.
Tumor suppressor WT1 on chromosome 11p13; WT2 region at 11p15.5 is linked to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
WAGR: deletion at 11p13 causing Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and developmental delay.
Denys-Drash: WT1 mutation with early nephrotic syndrome (diffuse mesangial sclerosis), gonadal dysgenesis, and Wilms tumor.
Beckwith-Wiedemann: macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihyperplasia, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycemia, and risk of Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.
Urothelial carcinoma is the most common bladder cancer; it also arises in the renal pelvis and ureter.
Classic sign: painless gross hematuria in an older adult.
Two paths: papillary tumors (most are low grade, recur often, and rarely invade) and flat carcinoma in situ (high grade, likely to invade).
The whole urothelium is exposed to the same urine carcinogens, so tumors are often multifocal and recur in new places.
Risk factors: smoking (most important), aromatic amines from dye, rubber, and leather industries, cyclophosphamide, phenacetin.
Squamous cell carcinoma: chronic irritation from Schistosoma haematobium eggs, long-term catheters, or stones causes squamous metaplasia that turns malignant.
Adenocarcinoma: arises from urachal remnants at the bladder dome or in bladder exstrophy.

Malignant; renal vein and IVC invasion, lung and bone spread
Papillae with foamy macrophages in the cores

tricks.label: WAGR
tricks.text: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, Range of developmental delays, from a deletion at 11p13.

tricks.label: Problems in your Pee SAC
tricks.text: Urothelial carcinoma risk factors: Phenacetin, Smoking, Aromatic amines (aniline dyes), Cyclophosphamide.

tricks.label: RCC makes hormones
tricks.text: Think of the kidney's own products plus a few extras: erythropoietin gives polycythemia, renin gives hypertension, and PTHrP gives hypercalcemia.

highYield: Older smoker with hematuria, a flank mass, and polycythemia: renal cell carcinoma making erythropoietin.
Golden-yellow kidney tumor with clear cells and VHL loss on 3p: clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
Bilateral renal cell carcinomas with cerebellar hemangioblastoma: von Hippel-Lindau disease.
Renal cell carcinoma likes to invade the renal vein and IVC and spread to lung and bone.
Brown kidney mass with a central stellate scar and mitochondria-rich cells: oncocytoma, which is benign.
A 3-year-old with a large unilateral flank mass and triphasic histology: Wilms tumor.
Child with aniridia should be screened for Wilms tumor (WAGR).
Painless gross hematuria in an older smoker: urothelial carcinoma until proven otherwise.
pitfalls: Clear cell and papillary RCC come from the proximal tubule; chromophobe RCC and oncocytoma come from intercalated cells.

Wilms tumor and neuroblastoma both give abdominal masses in young children; Wilms arises in the kidney, while neuroblastoma arises from adrenal or sympathetic tissue, can cross the midline, and raises urine catecholamine metabolites.
Flat carcinoma in situ looks less dramatic than a papillary tumor but is high grade and more likely to invade.
Schistosoma haematobium is linked to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, not urothelial carcinoma.

dumps.p: Draw a kidney with a renal cell carcinoma at one pole. Show where it spreads, then list the hormones it can make and what each one causes.
l: Clear cell type arises from proximal tubule cells
Golden-yellow cut surface with hemorrhage and necrosis
VHL loss on chromosome 3p
Grows into renal vein and inferior vena cava
Left renal vein blockage can cause a left varicocele
Spreads to lung and bone
Erythropoietin causes polycythemia
PTHrP causes hypercalcemia; renin causes hypertension
Risk: smoking, obesity, hypertension, dialysis cysts, VHL

l: Urothelial carcinoma is the most common type
Urothelial risk: smoking, aromatic amine dyes, cyclophosphamide, phenacetin
Papillary low-grade tumors recur often; flat CIS is high grade
Multifocal because all the urothelium sees the same carcinogens
Classic sign: painless gross hematuria
Squamous: Schistosoma haematobium, catheters, stones, squamous metaplasia
Adenocarcinoma: urachal remnant at the dome, bladder exstrophy

summary: This unit covers urinary tract infections from the urethra to the kidney: urethritis, cystitis, and acute pyelonephritis. Exam items ask you to tell the levels apart by symptoms and urine findings, name the likely organism, explain who is at risk, and predict complications.

points: Most UTIs are ascending: gut bacteria colonize the periurethral area, climb the urethra, and reach the bladder.
E. coli causes most UTIs; P fimbriae help uropathogenic strains bind urothelium and reach the kidney.
Other organisms: Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young sexually active women), Proteus and Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and hospital gram-negative rods.
Proteus makes urease, which splits urea to ammonia, makes urine alkaline, and favors struvite stones.
Hematogenous spread to the kidney is less common and is seen with bacteremia such as Staphylococcus aureus.
Risk factors: female sex (short urethra close to the anus), sexual intercourse, pregnancy, urinary catheters, diabetes, and obstruction.
Symptoms: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, sometimes hematuria.
No fever, no flank pain, and no WBC casts, because the kidney is not involved.
Urine: pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and a positive nitrite test with most gram-negative rods.
Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus usually do not convert nitrate to nitrite, so the nitrite test can be negative.
Usually ascending infection; risk rises with vesicoureteral reflux, obstruction, pregnancy, diabetes, and catheters.
Fever, chills, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, nausea, often with cystitis symptoms first.
WBC casts form in the tubules and prove the infection is in the kidney.
Histology: patchy neutrophilic inflammation of the interstitium with neutrophils filling tubules; glomeruli are spared early.
Complications: papillary necrosis (diabetes, obstruction), pyonephrosis (pus filling a blocked collecting system), perinephric abscess, and sepsis.
Repeated episodes with reflux or obstruction lead to chronic pyelonephritis.
Gonococcal urethritis: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus seen inside neutrophils on Gram stain.
Gonococcal discharge is heavy and purulent and starts a few days after exposure.
Nongonococcal urethritis: Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars D to K) most often; also Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas.
Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism not seen on Gram stain; discharge is scant and watery, and many infections cause no symptoms.
Nucleic acid amplification testing detects both; coinfection is common.
Gonococcal pili change their antigens, so infection does not leave lasting immunity and reinfection is common.
Men: epididymitis (the usual cause in younger sexually active men) and prostatitis.
Women: cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease, leading to infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).
Chlamydia can trigger reactive arthritis: arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis, often in HLA-B27 positive people.
Disseminated gonococcal infection causes septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions.

tricks.label: Reactive arthritis: can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree
tricks.text: Conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis after Chlamydia (or a GI infection), often in HLA-B27 positive people.

tricks.label: Fever and casts climb to the kidney
tricks.text: Bladder infection gives burning and urgency only. Add fever, flank pain, and WBC casts and the infection has reached the kidney.

tricks.label: Sterile pyuria
tricks.text: WBCs in the urine with a negative routine culture: think Chlamydia or gonococcal urethritis, interstitial nephritis, or renal tuberculosis.

highYield: E. coli is the most common cause of cystitis and pyelonephritis; P fimbriae aid ascent to the kidney.
Young sexually active woman with cystitis and a nitrite-negative urine: think Staphylococcus saprophyticus.
Alkaline urine and struvite stones: urease-positive Proteus.
Fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness, and WBC casts: acute pyelonephritis.
Diabetic with pyelonephritis who passes tissue in the urine: papillary necrosis.
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci in urethral pus: gonococcal urethritis.
Scant discharge with neutrophils but no organisms on Gram stain: Chlamydia trachomatis.
Urethritis followed by arthritis and conjunctivitis: reactive arthritis.
pitfalls: Cystitis and pyelonephritis can both cause dysuria; fever, flank pain, and WBC casts mean the kidney is involved.
A negative nitrite test does not rule out UTI; Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus often do not make nitrite.
Chlamydia does not appear on Gram stain because it lives inside cells and stains poorly; a Gram stain showing only neutrophils fits Chlamydia.
Pyonephrosis is pus in an obstructed collecting system; a perinephric abscess is pus that has broken through the capsule into the fat around the kidney.

dumps.p: Draw the urinary tract from urethra to kidney. Mark urethritis, cystitis, and pyelonephritis, and beside each write its symptoms, organisms, and urine findings.
l: Urethritis: dysuria with discharge; gonorrhea or chlamydia
Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, no fever
Cystitis organisms: E. coli, S. saprophyticus, Proteus, Klebsiella
Pyelonephritis: fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness
WBC casts only with kidney involvement
Most infections ascend from the urethra
Risk factors: female sex, intercourse, pregnancy, catheters, diabetes, obstruction, reflux

dumps.p: Make a two-column table comparing gonococcal and chlamydial urethritis. Include the organism, Gram stain, discharge, timing, and complications in men and women.
l: Gonorrhea: gram-negative intracellular diplococci
Chlamydia: obligate intracellular, not seen on Gram stain
Gonorrhea: heavy purulent discharge after a few days
Chlamydia: scant or no discharge, often silent
Both diagnosed by nucleic acid amplification testing
Men: epididymitis and prostatitis
Women: PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis
Chlamydia: reactive arthritis; gonorrhea: disseminated infection with septic arthritis
